alternatives.transcript: Today we're going back in time — about 5,000 years. The topic is cuneiform, the world's oldest writing system. Have you ever seen images of it? Cuneiform... I think I see this in a museum. It looks like... like small triangles or arrows, on clay tablet? Exactly right! It was pressed into wet clay using a reed stylus. The wedge-shaped marks are called cuneiform — from Latin, meaning wedge-shaped. Why do you think they used clay? Because... clay is easy to find? And you can write on it when it is wet and then it becomes... becomes hard. So it is like... like early paper? Brilliant analogy — like early paper! And clay preserved incredibly well — we have 5,000-year-old tablets that are perfectly readable today. That is really incredible. Um... who invented this writing? Was it one person or... or many people across the time? Great question — actually, 'invented' is debated. Writing emerged gradually in Mesopotamia — modern Iraq — among the Sumerian people, mainly to keep trade records. Trade records? So the first writing was not for... not for poetry or religion but for... for business? That surprises me. It surprises most people! The earliest tablets record things like '29 goats received', '15 jars of oil'. Very practical. Do you think writing changed human civilization? Yes, absolutely. Without writing, people can only remember what they... what they keep in the head. With writing you can store knowledge for future generations. Like a... like a memory outside the brain. I love that metaphor — a memory outside the brain! That's a very sophisticated thought. Can you use 'transmit' in a sentence about writing? Uh... writing allows people to transmit knowledge... across generations? Without writing, the knowledge... the knowledge dies when the person dies. Perfect sentence! Very philosophical. Now, do you know any other ancient writing systems? Yes, I know Egyptian hieroglyphics. And also Chinese characters — they are very old too. And in my country we have old... old Slavic script called Glagolitic. Glagolitic! Fascinating — I didn't know that. Can you tell me more about it? It was created in ninth century for Slavic languages by two Byzantine monks — Cyril and Methodius. Today we use Cyrillic alphabet which is named after Cyril. You just taught me something new! That's wonderful — you're the expert now. How does it feel to share knowledge about your own culture? It feels good! I think in these conversations I learn English but I also learn about the world and I can share my own... my own perspective.
